newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. vetoes Boutros-Ghali for new U.N. term.
newsitem.headline: U.S. vetoes Boutros-Ghali for new U.N. term.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday vetoed a second term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali as secretary-general of the United Nations, standing alone against all other 14 members of the Security Council.

The vote, at the request of the United States, was by secret ballot on a resolution sponsored by 10 of the 15 Security Council members. It would have put Boutros-Ghali, a 74-year-old Egyptian, in office for another five years, until 2001.
Washington's veto will open the way for other candidates to enter the race for a five-year term as secretary-general beginning January 1, Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia said.

The council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa, on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.
But Tuesday's vote did not exclude the prospect of Boutros-Ghali's name being submitted again, and African members of the council -- Egypt, Botswana and Guinea-Bissau -- indicated they might do that.

"We would like to make it very clear that we are very pleased with the result. It proves that the whole world was behind Africa and behind the candidate that Africa chose, which is the current secretary-general," Egyptian ambassador Nabil Elaraby said.
Guinea-Bissau's ambassador, Alfredo Lopes Cabral, said: "If you go back to the process of electing a secretary-general you will see that some of them who have served have been vetoed before."
Boutros-Ghali's spokeswoman, Sylvana Foa, told reporters: "The secretary-general was gratified and he really appreciates the overwhelming support shown by the U.N. members states."

U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said she cast the negative vote on "standing instructions" from Secretary of State Warren Christopher, implying she would continue to veto Boutros-Ghali if his name was resubmitted.
She said she spoke to Christopher's party in Beijing and he agreed "we get on with the process of selecting a new secretary-general."
"The United States has no candidate," Albright said. "We are waiting for the African countries to come forward with a list of viable candidates."
Washington announced in June it intended to block Boutros-Ghali's re-election, saying the United Nations needed new leadership to implement reforms.
U.S. officials also say the Republican-dominated U.S. Congress will not provide the money needed to pay off $1.4 billion in U.S. dues to the world body unless Boutros-Ghali is replaced.

Wisnumurti told reporters that "in a vote taken by secret ballot the draft received 14 votes in favour, one vote against and no abstentions. Since the negative vote was cast by a permanent member, the draft resolution was not adopted."
He said the ballots were marked to distinguish the council's five permanent members with veto power -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China -- from the 10 non-permanent members.

"Upon the receipt of the names of candidates from the African countries or the Organisation of Africa Unity, the president will draw up a list," he said. Diplomats said they did not expect any further voting until later this week, or perhaps next week.
The 14 states voting for the secretary-general were France, Britain, Russia, China, Botswana, Chile, Egypt, Germany, Guinea-Bissau, Honduras, Indonesia, Italy, South Korea and Poland.
Four of them -- Britain, Italy, South Korea and Poland -- did not sponsor the resolution, indicating they might be willing to move on to another candidate.

Among African diplomats mentioned as potential candidates are Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; Salim A. Salim of Tanzania, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity; Senegalese President Abdou Diouf; and Amara Essy, the Ivory Coast foreign minister.
